notes: Timbr models concepts as first-class ontology entities; Snowflake models them as semantic-view tables. Both covered the agreed concept list.
Timbr states relationships explicitly in the ontology, including hierarchies; Snowflake expresses relationships as view joins, which covers common cases but is less explicit for deep hierarchies.
Both define metrics once and reuse them. Timbr metrics attach to ontology concepts; Snowflake metrics attach to semantic views and are consumed natively by Cortex Analyst.

On the shared question set both produced structurally correct queries for the clear majority of questions; failures on both sides were dominated by genuinely ambiguous questions rather than modeling gaps.

Timbr queries are SQL against ontology concepts, reusable in any SQL tool. Snowflake semantic views are queried through Cortex Analyst/Agents rather than directly in SQL, which fits agent use cases but not ad-hoc SQL users.
Timbr is an additional governed layer to deploy, secure and upgrade. Semantic views are native Snowflake objects with no extra platform footprint.
Semantic views are the native input to Cortex Analyst and Cortex Agents. Timbr integrates at the SQL layer, so agent experiences are built on top rather than consumed natively.
Both inherit Snowflake data access controls. Timbr adds ontology-level governance concepts; Snowflake governs through native object privileges and semantic-view definitions.

The ontology up-front modeling investment is materially higher: concepts, hierarchies and relationships must be designed before querying pays off. Semantic views can be built incrementally per use case.
Semantic views answered governed questions quickly for a single domain. Timbr's payoff grows with cross-domain reuse of the shared ontology.
